In my experience, the whole "gun control debate" tends to be very binary. I think most of the arguments between liberals and conservatives focus on the issue of self defense or gun related crime. I always felt in my gut there was another reason I was so passionate about an individual's right to bear arms, but I could never articulate it until the other day:

Individual sovereignty

Max Weber, one of the fathers of the field of sociology, rightly pointed out that all State authority ultimately rests on the implicit threat of violence, and part of what makes a state a state is successfully monopolizing the "legitimate" use of violence against its own citizens and others. A state might try to legitimize their violence through various means, be it claiming the will of God, or the will of the majority through voting, or whatever, (whether it can ever truly be legitimate is another issue), but the core equation still remains:

violence = power

As an individualist, owning a weapon is more than just self-defense, it's a means of asserting my individual sovereignty over my own person. It's a way of saying I am not property of the state and I have some element of power to enforce that freedom.

I think this is lost on people when they're talking about banning the private ownership of firearms. They don't understand that what they're really advocating is slavery.

Sure it's not the vivid slavery of the past, with the ever present chains, but rather it's a more subtle slavery. You're removing the last vestiges of power from a populace and ensuring only their masters have that power.

It is an interesting point of view. If owning a gun equates to power then the more guns you own means the more power you have. My thought is that your sense of individual sovereignty is just an illusion because we as an individual can never own as many arsenal as the state.

Instead of just # of guns in your possession being the metric for power, I think it would be more accurate to say that power is determined by your ability to utilize violence.

In this case, having more guns wouldn't increase a single individual's power if they can only use one of them at a time.

You are correct that an individual can never have an arsenal as large as the state, but I would disagree with the conclusion that this makes sovereignty an illusion.

Let's look at national sovereignty for a moment as I think I can use it to illustrate both points:

Take the nation of Luxembourg for example. According to a quick look on Wikipedia, it has a military of roughly 800 soldiers. Luxembourg is far less powerful than the United States. Technically, the US military has the power to strike any place on the planet within hours. (Ranging from missile strikes, to bombers, to deploying soldiers. I say technically* because I'm just talking about the hypothetical technical ability to do something operating in a vacuum.)

Despite this vast difference in power between the US and Luxembourg, Luxembourg is still a sovereign nation.

The US could, if it really wanted to, destroy Luxembourg at any moment, at which point it would no longer be a sovereign nation. I would argue that this exact same fact holds true for individual sovereignty.

I will never have the same kind of violence power as the State, and yet I am still a sovereign individual. The State could crush me at any moment with it's power, at which point I would be dead and it wouldn't matter, but at least I would die as a sovereign individual and I believe there is intrinsic value in that.

I understand your point of view. I guess illusion was not quite the right word, fragile maybe better to describe it because that individual sovereignty can be taken away by the state at any moment. Waco, Saddam Husein and Osama for examples.

The question for now, is it worth to hold on to that fragile and fleeting notion of sovereignty over the risk of mass shooting ?

Luxembourg is also a good example for a sovereignty, if Luxembourg has such a minuscule army yet still a sovereign nation, would it be possible for an person without a gun to have the individual sovereignty ?

In response to your 2nd question about can an individual (or nation) have sovereignty without weapons, I guess I would have to echo what /u/Kromulent said below: Their existence depends on the whim and disposition of others. There's a list of countries without a military and I would argue that they continue to exist at the will of any country with a military. Should someone with force bother to invade they would be destroyed unless someone else with force decided to come to their aid. Same applies for individuals.

As for the first question, "is it worth it to hold onto this fragile notion of sovereignty in the risk of mass shootings?" I would say yes. Why?

  1. First off, I think the whole argument of "should we or should we not forcefully violate a mass of individuals basic human rights by disarming them" is not an ethical argument in the first place.

  2. Ignoring point 1., I believe statistically the chances of dying in a mass shooting incident, while popular on sensationalist news sites, is relatively small compared to more prevalent causes of death. In 2013, 32,719 people in the US died in car related incidents. That same year, according to the CDC, 611,105 people died from heart disease, 584,881 died from cancer, 149,205 died from lower respiratory issues.

  3. Following from point 2, I think statistically the number of State related deaths (death from war related violence and police brutality) has a long track record of being much higher historically than any dangers posed by armed individual citizens. Removing any form of check on this violence, regardless of how fragile or hopeless, would not be moving in the right direction.

I get what you are saying and I'd like to offer a slight restatement of this view.

The word you are looking for is coercion. It's the ability to make somebody do something that they otherwise would not do. Violence, and the threat of violence, is one form of coercion. Shaming is also coercion. Even lying is coercion. There is a very broad spectrum here.

The ability to coerce others, and to resist the coercion of others, is power.

Being powerless against the government is a big problem, but it's only part of the overall picture. Being powerless against one another is a smaller scale example of the same problem, and the same model scales up very nicely.

Consider a robbery; at the moment a robbery begins, it is literally an act of enslavement. "Hey, you there. Do not leave. Do exactly what I say. You must obey me". Perhaps the enslavement ends a half-minute later with the loss of a wallet. Perhaps it ends with a beating, or a sexual assault, or it grows to include others in your home. To be powerless in the face of this risk is to be made subservient within one's own society. We simply exist at the pleasure of others, to be selected and abused at any time.

Most people handle this by simply not dealing with it. They imagine the risk is not real, or that they have some special power to exempt themselves. Actually dealing with it in a sensible way is very hard, and few people rise to that. In fairness, most of us will get through most of our lives without facing personal violence like this at all. It only matters when the bad day finally comes around.

The foundation of our understanding of civil rights - equality under the law, the pursuit of happiness, the dignity of the individual - depends upon each person's ability to preserve their dignity, to resist enslavement, to enter each day as one among equals. If you cannot wield power enough to defend your own skin your equality depends merely upon the mood of those around you.

Extend this same model to the relationship between people and governments and it still works very well. It's not enough to be able to hold our own with a well-tempered government which is inclined to treat us fairly. If we intend to be free, we must be able to hold our own even against a government that finds us unpopular, unlikeable, undesirable. Otherwise we exist only at their pleasure.

The counterpoint of the model works nicely too. In person-to-person interaction, you do not need to fight like a Navy SEAL, you just need to present enough risk to make it no longer worthwhile to bother you. When dealing with the government, we only find them questioning the utility on no-knock SWAT raids only after so many turn into horrific gunfights involving innocent homeowners. When the innocent homeowners simply yielded like sheep, the mistakes were so much easier to ignore. Armed citizens can still be pushed around and abused, but it's more more dangerous and expensive.

You only retain the rights you can defend. Everything else is a gift, a license, and indulgence that can be revoked on a whim. Armed people are more able to preserve more of their rights in their interactions with others, including their interactions with their government.

Keep in mind, this is a theoretical model. In practice, everything is greatly complicated and the answers are never quite so simple. But I can promise you this - if you are legally armed, and interacting with a grouchy cop wearing a live body camera, you are in a different world than if you are unarmed and interacting with a grouchy cop where nobody to see what really happens. That's the practical difference.
